reports.name: Junior Caminero
reports.published_report: Forty-six home runs from a 23-year-old is the headline, and the Statcast profile says it's load-bearing: a 93.1 mph average exit velocity and 50.8% hard-hit rate put him in rarefied contact-quality company, and a .512 xSLG translates to exactly this kind of power output in a full season. The walk rate is a quiet strength at 12.4%, well above league average, and the strikeout rate of 18.4% is genuinely tidy for a bat with this much loft. The one real tension in the profile is defense: a 1st-percentile OAA at third base means his value lives entirely in that bat, and if the position becomes untenable, he's a DH whose offense has to carry everything. It does, for now.

reports.name: Pete Crow-Armstrong
reports.published_report: The .365 xwOBA and 49.4% hard-hit rate tell you the contact quality is elite, and the 12.3% barrel rate confirms the power translates. The problem is a 34.0% chase rate that suppresses his actual batting average well below what the underlying contact suggests, which is why xBA sits at .256 while xwOBA lives in the 90th percentile — he's leaking value at the plate he doesn't have to leak. What saves the profile is 29.5 ft/s sprint speed, 12.3% walk rate, and a projected 39 stolen bases, enough to make a .277/.372/.522 line with 34 home runs feel conservative if he ever tightens his zone decisions, and enough to keep him a genuine everyday contributor even if he doesn't.

reports.name: Jacob Misiorowski
reports.published_report: A 1.94 xERA and 40.6% strikeout rate at this point in a career isn't a profile you talk around. Misiorowski is posting a 38.3% whiff rate and a 3.5% barrel rate allowed, and those two numbers together tell you why hitters aren't doing damage — they're not even making real contact. The 6.0% walk rate is the only place the profile breathes, sitting in the 87th percentile, meaning the command is good without being elite, and if it slips toward the middle of the zone he's still a strikeout machine but hitters will start getting something to hit. ValuCast projects 182.6 innings of a 2.12 ERA and 270 strikeouts, which is exactly what a 100.6 mph fastball with 2628 rpm behind it, deployed by someone who already knows how to miss bats at scale, looks like when it carries into a full season.

reports.name: Bobby Witt Jr.
reports.published_report: The xBA sits at .302 at the 100th percentile, and that's before you factor in what 30.2 ft/s does to routine grounders. The contact quality is elite on both ends: 92.8 mph average exit velocity, 52.5% hard-hit rate, and an xSLG of .510 that the projection's .462 SLG hasn't fully caught up to yet. The one real wrinkle is a 33.0% chase rate that keeps him in the bottom third of the league for plate discipline, and if pitchers ever figure out how to consistently exploit that, the strikeout rate climbs and the walk rate softens from the already-modest 10.2%. For now, though, the speed and contact quality together make the projection's 42 stolen bases and .284 AVG look conservative rather than optimistic, and this profile reads as a true star at the position rather than a compiler.

reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: The .408 xwOBA and 2.73 xERA living in the same body is the whole argument. As a hitter, the contact quality is genuinely elite, 93.4 mph average exit velocity and a 16.6% barrel rate, and a 13.8% walk rate that keeps the .393 OBP honest even with a 22.8% strikeout rate that costs him nothing at this production level. On the mound, the 98.1 mph fastball paired with a 30.4% whiff rate gives him a strikeout profile that plays, and hitters are barreling him at just 3.8%, which explains why the underlying ERA picture looks like an ace. The ValuCast projection of 38 home runs and a .942 OPS across 693 plate appearances assumes he handles the DH workload cleanly and logs meaningful innings, and the whole profile hinges on staying on both sides of the lineup card — if the pitching role contracts or disappears, you still have a monster hitter, but you lose the thing that makes him singular.

reports.name: James Wood
reports.published_report: The contact-and-power profile here is as loud as it gets: a 20.8% barrel rate and a 95.1 mph average exit velocity both sitting at the 100th percentile, with an xSLG of .585 that says the projection's .523 SLG is conservative. Wood also runs a 16.8% walk rate that almost no hitter at this level can match. The whole thing hinges on whether a 28.6% strikeout rate, bottom 12% of the league, ever comes down, because at the current whiff rate the gap between what he should hit and what he actually hits stays wide. If it does compress even modestly, you're talking about a legitimate MVP-caliber season out of a 23-year-old; if it doesn't, the .387 OBP and the power still make him a middle-of-the-order force, just a noisier one.

reports.name: Sal Stewart
reports.published_report: Thirty-three projected home runs at 22 years old, and the Statcast profile explains exactly where they're coming from: a 14.0% barrel rate that grades in the 89th percentile, paired with an .xSLG of .468 that lines up cleanly with the projected .472 SLG. The xBA sits at .247 against an xwOBA of .345, which is the whole tension in the profile — he hits the ball hard enough to do real damage when he connects, but the contact quality doesn't spread evenly across the zone, and a 26.6% whiff rate says pitchers will keep finding the soft spots. If the 10.3% walk rate holds and the strikeouts stay manageable, the projection's .803 OPS is a reasonable landing spot; if the whiff rate climbs, the .255 AVG erodes and you're leaning on the power to carry him. Everyday corner bat with real offensive upside, as long as the barrel rate isn't just carrying a contact profile that's thinner than it looks.

reports.name: Yordan Alvarez
reports.published_report: The xwOBA is .464 and the xSLG is .688, both at the 100th percentile, which means the Statcast profile isn't arguing about whether he's elite — it's arguing about degree. A 18.1% barrel rate paired with a 15.7% walk rate is the combination that makes the projection's .429 OBP and 45 home runs feel like a description rather than a hope. He doesn't need to run, and at 25.1 ft/s he can't, because the contact quality does everything, and a 17.1% strikeout rate means he's rarely handing at-bats back. The one thing to watch is the 28.1% chase rate, which sits in merely ordinary territory; if pitchers ever find a way to exploit it consistently, the walk rate compresses and the whole offensive profile gets a little less absurd, though "a little less absurd" still leaves plenty of room.

reports.name: Jackson Merrill
reports.published_report: The power contact profile is legitimate and the speed is genuine, but the zone judgment hasn't caught up. Merrill's .468 xSLG and 46.9% hard-hit rate say the raw damage is there, yet a 36.5% chase rate sitting in the 15th percentile poisons the walk column down to 6.3% and keeps the projection at .247/.298/.425 despite bat-to-ball skills that deserve better. At 23, with sprint speed at 28.9 ft/s and a fielding profile that grades out well, the floor is a useful multi-category contributor. The ceiling depends entirely on whether he can lay off breaking stuff down and away, because if that chase rate drops into average range, the .468 xSLG starts showing up in the actual line and you're looking at a genuine everyday player rather than a slightly frustrating one.

The whole profile hinges on whether that command holds as he climbs, because if the walks tick up and the strikeout rate softens even slightly, you're looking at a back-end starter rather than a genuine front-line piece.

Neto's contact profile is genuinely ugly, a 36.9% chase rate and 33.5% whiff rate that land in the 13th and 9th percentiles respectively, but when he does connect, the barrel number sits at the 79th percentile, which is why the projection still has him at 27 home runs across 707 plate appearances despite an xBA of .198. The .225 AVG in the projection isn't pessimism; it's the chase rate translating honestly. Everything hinges on whether the power frequency holds up against pitchers who've figured out how to exploit that zone-expansion tendency, because if the barrel rate regresses even modestly, what's left is a shortstop with an empty .308 OBP.

reports.name: Pete Alonso
reports.published_report: The contact metrics and the raw power say two different things, and knowing which one to trust is the whole read. His average exit velocity sits at 94.1 mph with 56.0% of balls classified as hard-hit, both at the 98th percentile, and an xSLG of .531 that the projection simply can't fully cash — 35 projected home runs against contact that good is a conservative translation, not a ceiling. The 24.5% strikeout rate is the cost, a real drag on a .344 OBP that would be even fatter if he made more consistent contact, and pitchers who can manufacture whiffs at 27.0% against him will keep the batting average suppressed around that .251 projection. The whole profile hinges on lineup protection in Baltimore; if he's hitting fourth behind genuine threats, the walk rate stays honest at 11.5% and the power plays, and if he's not, pitchers go around him and the .817 OPS looks like a ceiling rather than a floor.

reports.name: Juan Soto
reports.published_report: The .422 xwOBA tells you almost everything you need to know, and the 19.8% chase rate tells you why it's sustainable. Soto's contact quality sits at the very top of the league, with an xSLG of .589 and a barrel rate of 14.3%, while his 17.5% walk rate keeps pitchers from ever getting comfortable attacking him. The projection's .410 OBP and .948 OPS across 489 PA aren't optimistic; they're just what happens when a hitter with this chase profile and this much raw contact quality stays healthy. Sprint speed at 25.9 ft/s is a real limitation, so the ceiling here is defined entirely by the bat, and the bat is about as clean a profile as you'll find.

reports.name: Liam Doyle
reports.published_report: 100 strikeouts in 76 AA innings is the loud part of this profile, and the 11.8 K/9 translates to roughly 9.3 at the MLB level, a tick above average. The walk rate is the problem: 43 walks in those same 76 innings, a 5.1 BB/9 at AA that softens to something closer to 4.7 against big-league competition, nearly a run and a half above what a league-average starter allows. The K-BB% at 17% looks fine against his AA peers, but the MLB-equivalent lands at 12.8%, just below the 13.5% baseline, which means all that strikeout upside is getting eaten alive by free passes before it ever shows up in results. If he tightens the zone and the swing-and-miss holds, he's a back-end rotation piece; if the command stays here, there's not much rotation left to talk about.

At 12.0% BB%, Karros is getting on base in a way the raw slash line doesn't fully advertise, and the .338 xwOBA suggests he's been roughly as valuable as a .358 OBP hitter deserves to be. The contact quality sits right around average, 89.8 mph exit velocity and 7.8% barrel rate, nothing that screams impact, but a 24.4% chase rate in the 84th percentile tells you the walks are earned, not gifted by pitchers losing the zone. The projection's .264/.358/.414 line in 514 PA reads like a solid second-division regular at a premium position, maybe a tick better if the plate discipline holds in a park that can inflate the bad outcomes along with the good ones.

reports.name: Connelly Early
reports.published_report: The gap between a 3.51 ERA projection and a 4.31 xERA is the whole argument here, and it's not an encouraging one. Early's Statcast contact profile is genuinely punishing — a 10.6% barrel rate and 40.9% hard-hit rate both sit well below the median, and hitters are squaring him up consistently enough that the underlying run-prevention math leans toward regression. His 31.4% chase rate gives him something to work with, but a 23.7% whiff rate means he's not finishing those expanded swings at a useful clip. If that chase-to-whiff disconnect holds, he profiles as a back-end rotation filler who gives Washington league-average length on a good day and early showers when his location slips.

reports.name: Kyle Schwarber
reports.published_report: The 17.7% barrel rate tells you what he is: a wrecking ball who hits the ball harder than almost anyone in the sport, with a 93.1 mph average exit velocity and a 15.4% walk rate that keeps pitchers from working around the damage. The .373 xwOBA says the production is earned, not luck-adjacent. The catch is the 34.1% strikeout rate, which sits at the bottom of the league, and the profile only holds together because the contact he does make is so punishing that the outs between the walks and the barrels become manageable. Project 46 home runs in 694 plate appearances and the math is straightforward: if the strikeouts spike further and the barrel rate softens, the batting average falls below .242 and the whole offensive case erodes quickly, but as long as the exit velocity holds, the .889 OPS is a reasonable floor.

reports.name: Justin Wrobleski
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the whole argument here: 5.5 BB% puts him at the 92nd percentile, and it's doing a lot of lifting for a pitcher whose 19.1 K% and 19.4 Whiff% both sit in the bottom quarter of the league. He gets chases at a respectable 31.8% clip, so hitters aren't simply ignoring him, but the contact they do make is punishing, with a 43.1% Hard-Hit rate that the .330 xwOBA and 4.63 xERA reflect honestly. The projection's 3.66 ERA and 1.16 WHIP read as a best-case scenario built on him continuing to limit free passes while the defense and sequencing behind him behave; if the command slips even modestly, the strikeout-to-contact profile has no margin to absorb it. Back-end starter with a clear ceiling, and a long reliever's floor if the zone command regresses.

reports.name: Karson Milbrandt
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate translates cleanly; the walk rate is where this profile earns its asterisk. Across AAA & AA in 2026, Milbrandt has punched out 103 batters in 84.3 innings, but he's also issued 51 walks, and that BB/9 translates to 4.9 at the MLB level while the league average sits at 3.2. The stuff is loud enough to keep him interesting. reports.name: Kahlil Watson
reports.published_report: The ISO is the loudest thing in this profile, and it creates a real tension: .219 at AAA with 14 home runs and 19 stolen bases is a legitimately interesting tool combination, but 89 strikeouts against 45 walks in 320 plate appearances translates to a 26.9% strikeout rate at the MLB level, and that gap from the 22.0% MLB average is wide enough to decide everything. The .367 OBP at AAA flatters him because a 14% walk rate won't fully survive the jump, and the MLB-equivalent translation pegs his BB% at 11.3 — still meaningfully above the 8.5% MLB baseline, but the foundation gets thinner if pitchers don't expand the zone for him. If the contact holds, you get a bench or platoon bat with legitimate pop and speed on the bases; if the strikeout rate balloons the way it can for left-handed hitters who swing hard in their first real MLB exposure, the floor is a depth piece without enough contact to stay in a lineup.

reports.name: Jackson Kent

The K-BB% of 20% across those levels translates to 14.5% in MLB terms, a tick above the league mean, which means the profile isn't built on strikeouts he doesn't quite own, his 10.0 K/9 in the minors comes back to 8.6 in translation, it's built on not giving hitters free passes. If the command holds in full-time big-league exposure, he's a multi-inning reliever with a real job; if it slips, 105 strikeouts don't leave enough margin to survive, and you're looking at a depth arm filling innings when someone goes down.

A .223 ISO across AA & A+ in 185 plate appearances translates to a .156 MLB-equivalent, and the MLB walk rate sits at 8.5% while his equivalent comes in at 7.1%, which tells you the discipline isn't going to carry him when the contact thins. The .297 OBP built on a 6% walk rate and a .263 BABIP leaves almost no margin, and twelve stolen bases across AA & A+ add a wrinkle without solving anything structural. The profile hinges entirely on whether the power stays loud enough at higher levels to compensate for an on-base game that currently doesn't exist, and if it doesn't, you're looking at a bench bat whose best asset is one tool that minor-league translations tend to compress.

reports.name: Brycen Mautz
reports.published_report: The 3.50 ERA is doing a lot of cosmetic work here. Translate Mautz's AAA walk rate to a major-league equivalent and you get 5.5 BB/9 against an MLB average of 3.2, a gap that swallows almost all of the strikeout value he creates. His 82 strikeouts in 79.7 innings at AAA look fine until you see the 58 walks sitting next to them, and the K-BB% percentile of 20 among qualified pitchers makes the command problem hard to explain away. If the walk rate tightens, there's a back-end arm in here somewhere; if it doesn't, the ERA won't stay that low.

reports.name: Riley Quick
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is loud, the walk rate is the whole problem. Across AA & A+ & A in 2026, Quick has 81 strikeouts in 58 innings, and the 12.6 K/9 translates to 8.9 at the MLB level, a tick above the 8.6 MLB mean. The translated BB/9 of 4.9, though, lands well north of the 3.2 MLB average, and that gap is what keeps a 4.00 ERA from meaning much. The K-BB% of 20% is genuinely strong at 22, but closing the gap between 4.9 and 3.2 is the whole hinge: if the walks tighten, there's a back-end starter scenario; if they don't, the ceiling collapses to depth arm and the floor is the same place.

reports.name: Cristofer Torin
reports.published_report: The contact is legitimate. At AA this season across 429 plate appearances, Torin is striking out just 11% of the time, which translates to a 15.9% K rate at the MLB level, well below the 22.0% mark that separates him from most hitters at that tier. The problem is everything around it: his .319 OBP sits at the 26th percentile among the prospect pool, the MLB-equivalent ISO comes out at .121 where the average sits at .150, and a .258 BABIP suggests the hit tool isn't carrying him to better outcomes than his contact rate deserves. If the power doesn't develop, you're left with a contact-first shortstop who can't get on base enough to make the role work, and the ceiling here is organizational depth rather than a regular.

reports.name: Trey Yesavage
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the whole argument. A 30.0% Whiff rate and a 3.37 xERA say the stuff plays, but an 11.9% BB% is quietly bleeding the profile dry, because you can't strand what you can't stop putting on base. The contact quality is genuinely suppressed and the swing-and-miss is there, yet the walks push his projection to a 3.78 ERA and 1.19 WHIP across 117.0 innings, which is the gap between a mid-rotation starter and a guy cycling in and out depending on his command week to week. If the walk rate comes down, the 3.37 xERA is the real ceiling and he's a legitimate front-half piece for Toronto; if it doesn't, 116 strikeouts against a leaky WHIP describes a back-end arm who needs his defense.

reports.name: Brandon Sproat
reports.published_report: The fastball sits 96.7 mph, which is loud, and then you see the 2046 rpm spin and understand why it hasn't mattered. Hitters are making hard contact at a 43.1% clip and barely chasing at 25.5%, which is about as damaging a pairing as a power arm can carry: the velocity draws the strikeouts (24.2 K%) but the walk rate at 11.6% bleeds the counts before he can get there, and the xERA at 4.86 is the honest summary of what happens when you throw hard with flat spin and no command. The projection at 5.07 ERA over 116.0 innings suggests an innings-eater role that doesn't really eat innings cleanly, with only 5 quality starts in the picture. Everything here hinges on whether that walk rate comes down, because the strikeout shape says mid-rotation starter if it does and long reliever if it doesn't.

reports.name: Felnin Celesten
reports.published_report: The surface numbers are loud: .294/.388/.501 across AA & A+ this season, 21 stolen bases, 15 home runs in 433 plate appearances. Celesten is 20 years old doing this at Double-A, and the .208 ISO across those levels is the kind of number that makes you sit up. The translation is where the tension lives — his 22% strikeout rate across AA & A+ renders to 25.8% in MLB context, a tick past the 22.0% MLB average, and his ISO translates to .145, essentially matching what a league-average bat produces once the level discount applies. If the hit tool holds up against better arms, you have a legitimate everyday shortstop; if the strikeout rate climbs and the batted-ball quality doesn't travel, the floor is organizational depth, and that's a long fall from where the current line sits.

reports.name: Michael King
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile and the projection are telling two very different stories, and that gap is the whole read. His xERA sits at 4.42 with a K% of 21.5 and a BB% of 9.8, contact and command numbers that belong to a back-end arm, yet ValuCast's projection has him at a 3.53 ERA over 183.4 innings. What explains the gap is the hard-hit number: a 32.6% Hard-Hit rate that looks alarming until you see the 87.3 mph average exit velocity sitting in the 79th percentile, meaning hitters are making loud contact that isn't finding the barrel, which keeps the actual damage below what the xERA implies. The walk rate is the lever that matters most here; if 9.8% drifts higher, there's no swing-and-miss buffer at 21.5% K% to absorb it, and the ERA follows the xERA north in a hurry.

reports.name: Steven Kwan
reports.published_report: The contact-and-walk game is genuinely elite; the power is a different conversation entirely. Kwan's 9.1% whiff rate sits at the very top of the leaderboard, his chase rate of 21.4% is in the 93rd percentile, and that discipline combination explains how an outfielder with an 83.6 mph average exit velocity and a 0.3% barrel rate can still carry a .274 xBA. The xSLG of .336 is 11th percentile, and the projection's four home runs across a full 621-PA season isn't pessimism — it's the honest translation of what that contact profile produces without any lift behind it. If the on-base skill holds, he's a useful everyday piece in Cleveland's lineup; if the pitching industry ever finds a way to neutralize him at the plate, there's very little thump left to fall back on.

reports.name: Alex Bregman
reports.published_report:
The Statcast profile is a study in contradictions. Bregman's plate discipline is genuinely elite, a 22.2% chase rate and 16.2% whiff rate that rank among the best in the league, but the contact that results sits in the bottom fifth: 4.2% barrel rate, 88.2 mph average exit velocity, .356 xSLG. He's getting to the ball and doing very little with it.

The projection lives in that gap, .249/.339/.390 with 18 home runs across 715 PA, the 10.7% walk rate keeping the OBP respectable while the power profile stays hollow. The fielding grades out beautifully at third, which matters for his floor, but this is a guy whose offensive ceiling hinges entirely on whether he can add loft or strength to contact he's already making at an above-average rate. If the exit velocity doesn't come back, the .339 OBP leaves him a serviceable regular and nothing more.

Farmelo has drawn those across AA & A+ in 479 plate appearances, with 31 stolen bases sitting underneath a .378 OBP that gives the speed real utility. The hitch is the power: a .196 ISO at the minor-league level translates to .139 at the majors, while the MLB average sits at .150, meaning the on-base skills have to carry the whole profile against better arms. If the plate discipline holds and the stolen bases travel up the ladder, there's a table-setter with genuine OBP skills; if the strikeout rate, 25% across AA & A+ and translating to 28.4% at the MLB level, balloons at Triple-A, what's left is a light-hitting center fielder with a thin margin for error.

reports.name: Ashton Izzi
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the whole argument. Across AAA & AA in 2026, Ashton Izzi has issued 26 walks in 97.7 innings, a 2.4 BB/9 that translates to a 2.8 MLB-equivalent figure, comfortably under what big-league hitters typically see, and sitting in the 94th percentile among his pitching pool. The problem is everything else: his 7.7 K/9 across AAA & AA translates to 7.1 at the MLB level, well short of average, and a 5.1 ERA over 21 starts doesn't let you pretend the command is hiding a dominant arm. If the strike-throwing holds and he adds swing-and-miss to the profile, there's a back-end rotation floor here; if the strikeout rate stays where it is, the control becomes the one calling card on a depth arm.

reports.name: Josh Stephan
reports.published_report: The walk rate is doing real work here, and everything else is keeping up just enough. At AAA in 2026, 31 walks across 108 innings translates to a 92nd-percentile BB/9 among pitchers with meaningful samples, and the MLB equivalent puts that at 2.9 per nine, a tick better than the league mean. The trouble is the strikeouts: 102 punchouts in those same 108 innings look fine in isolation, but they translate to 7.8 per nine against a major-league context of 8.6, and the 5.20 ERA at AAA suggests the stuff isn't missing bats often enough to hold up when contact finds grass. If the control holds and the strikeout rate inches toward league average, you've got a back-end starter or long-man who earns a rotation spot in a thin year; if it doesn't, the floor is exactly what the ceiling says, a depth arm who commands the zone without the swing-and-miss to survive.

reports.name: Ben Kudrna
reports.published_report:
Two innings. That's the entire current AAA sample, and it's doing almost no work here.

What the translation shows isn't alarming but isn't encouraging: a K/9 that matches the MLB average exactly at 8.6, a BB/9 of 3.8 where the average sits at 3.2, and a K-BB% of 12.4 when the typical MLB starter lands at 13.5. If the strikeout rate doesn't climb and the walks stay where they are, the profile resolves as a depth arm, which is exactly where the ceiling lands anyway. The honest read here is that 2.0 IP can't tell you much, and ValuCast's rankings reflect that uncertainty, sliding him six spots in three days.
